name: Omar Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar, 43, and I carry tools and help with wiring and repairs while the experienced electrician checks what I do. I finished a vocational certificate after leaving supermarket stock work, but I'm still a junior, slower and less skilled than the rest. Our firm's starter pay is higher than most, and years of two wages left my partner and me with a year's expenses saved. We have children aged seven and eleven and a mortgage; I've never used AI and would rather study a paper drawing with somebody patient beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm happy to learn the wiring before we hold another discussion about machines. I've never used AI and I don't want a new app for every small part of the day. A patient supervisor and a clear drawing do more for me than another screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job and money feel secure in that picture. The firm's starter pay is higher than most, our household has a year's expenses saved, and there are plenty of nearby electrical employers. I still need supervision, but I don't need to pretend I'm an expert to feel that we can cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the supervised wiring and repair tasks. Starting now I'd take my course folder to the yard twice a week and ask the senior electrician about one drawing before we left for a job. Through the first year I'd keep learning that familiar way rather than buy software I wouldn't use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with room to learn slowly and properly. I don't enjoy being a beginner at 43, but I can bear it without imagining the next bill knocking us over. I'd rather admit what I don't know than race to look current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you reach the trade at this age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to supervise stock at a supermarket and finished a vocational certificate when I decided to change direction. Electrical work is still new to my hands, and I'm below the experienced crew for speed and skill. Our family saved over years of two wages. I don't have to learn electrical work on an empty account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is in the household you are planning for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner has regular paid work, and our children are seven and eleven. We have a mortgage, so savings don't mean I can simply stop earning. They mean I can replace a broken appliance without putting the next payment at risk.

say: I'd focus on **learning wiring** before debating machines I have never used.
I'd prefer a **patient supervisor** and a clear drawing to another app.
think: Higher **starter pay** and a year's expenses saved make my own work and money feel secure.
I still need **supervision**, but plenty of nearby employers and our reserve protect the mortgage from a small setback.
do: Keep doing **supervised wiring** and repair tasks through the first year.
Bring my **course folder** twice weekly and ask the senior electrician about one drawing before jobs.
feel: **Calm**, with enough financial breathing room to admit his limits and learn at a manageable pace.
S0.quote: I don't have to learn electrical work on an empty account.
fieldNote: His **higher junior pay** and year-long reserve explain security without turning a vocational certificate into advanced qualifications or practical skill.
He maintains **resistant habits**, preferring paper and patient instruction rather than suddenly adopting AI to simplify the profile.

steps.text: Keep supervised repairs and review paper drawings with the senior twice weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the workers who know the jobs should have a say before software redraws the week. Faster booking isn't a reason to leave people without training or hours. I wouldn't tell the office staff to stop worrying just because I carry cable rather than answer the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own paid days to hold over the next few years because our physical installation work is booked well ahead. Our reserve and the other firms nearby give me further protection. Still, I'm uneasy watching the office work change first, and I don't trust a neat schedule if it quietly removes the time somebody spends teaching me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union branch's next meeting this month and ask for a written request covering paid training and time for junior checks. At work I'd keep my own paper record of the time the senior spent showing me tasks. In the first year I'd bring actual examples to the meeting rather than claim a shorter diary automatically meant safer or better work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about how the decisions get made. My own mortgage isn't in immediate danger, but I don't want the people with a smaller cushion to carry the whole cost. I can afford to speak without pretending I'm speaking for everybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the written request to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That required teaching happens in paid hours, and that a junior still gets the checks the work needs. I'd want workers consulted before their paid days were changed. I'd help make the request through the meeting; I couldn't promise the employer would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new scheduling system yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for my assignments on paper while the office handled the system. I've never used AI, and a busy repair day isn't when I want to start experimenting. If a slot was wrong, I'd tell the supervisor exactly what the task needed.

say: I'd ask for **worker involvement** before software changes paid days or teaching time.
I'd take **office worries** seriously even while my own work remains mainly physical.
think: I expect my **paid days** to hold because installation work is booked ahead, supported by savings and local options.
I'm uneasy about **office changes** and the possibility that a neat schedule hides lost time for junior teaching.
do: Attend the next **union meeting** this month and join a written request for paid teaching and checks.
Record **teaching time** on paper and bring actual examples to discussions during the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about decision-making and colleagues' exposure, with his own near-term income feeling secure.
S1.quote: Faster booking isn't a reason to leave people without training or hours.
fieldNote: His **social concern** differs from his own secure earnings; he does not assume colleagues have already lost jobs.
The **collective action** is an actual meeting and written request, while familiar paper assignments preserve his resistance to using AI.

steps.text: Join the union written request for paid training time and required junior checks
Keep supervised work and paper records of time needed for teaching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 isn't the same as a robot pulling cable that day. The capable robots follow around 2031, which is still close enough to plan for. I'd ask the union to talk about junior workers before a purchase decision has already decided their future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could fall once machines do the simple physical jobs I help with. A year's expenses saved gives my family more room than many, but it doesn't buy the twenty working years I might still need. I don't know whether another local firm would be hiring if the same change reached all of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union branch now to seek a written paid-training and redeployment plan from the employer. I'd keep the household reserve intact rather than spend it on a course before the job and funding were clear. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep doing paid supervised repairs where offered and check real advertised helper roles if my hours fell, applying only for stated pay and paid hours that met our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own work now, though I don't feel cornered tonight. I can take time over an offer, but I can't call the reserve a solution for the rest of my career. I'd sleep better after a real employer agreement than another speech about resilience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real redeployment plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Named tasks people would actually do, paid learning time, who would teach them and what hours and pay followed. I'd want to see the agreement, not just a list of courses. I'd also want the workers whose savings are smaller to have the same chance to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the reserve instead of paying for training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't yet know which paid job the course would lead to. I prefer a practical path with agreed teaching, and our family still has a mortgage. Keeping existing savings is different from suddenly earning a second wage.

say: I'd distinguish **thinking AI in 2028** from capable robots following around 2031.
I'd press for **junior workers** to be included before machine purchases decide staffing needs.
think: My **paid hours** could fall when robots do the simple physical tasks I help with.
A year's **savings** buys time, while nearby firms may face the same change and cannot be assumed to hire.
do: Seek a written **paid-training plan** through the union now, including actual tasks, pay and hours.
Keep the **existing reserve** intact while job and course funding remain unclear.
Continue **paid repairs** after 2028 and seek posted roles only if reduced hours and adequate stated terms justify applying.
feel: **Anxious** about his own employment, with enough resources to consider offers without feeling trapped tonight.
S2.quote: Keeping existing savings is different from suddenly earning a second wage.
fieldNote: He recognises **own-job risk** in later robot capability while retaining physical work in the first post-2028 year and uncertainty about local hiring.
Retaining the **existing reserve** is not tagged as new saving; action tags cover actual union requests, continued work and conditional job applications.

steps.text: Seek a written paid-training and redeployment plan through the union
Keep paid supervised repair work after 2028 where offered
Apply after 2028 for posted helper jobs if hours fall and stated pay covers bills
Check offered paid hours meet household bills before accepting a job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should let an employer teach the workers it already has. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and the robots around 2034, so I'd ask what practical skills we can learn before then. I'd still want paid training to be available to the person without my reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own income to remain secure over the next few years, with time to improve at the trade. I'd be 48 in 2031 and our children would be twelve and sixteen, so I'd still need wages well beyond that point. I'm uneasy about the later competition, not expecting an immediate household crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the employer this month to put me on the next practical installation class as part of my paid week. I'd enrol if the fees and paid time were agreed, with a named senior checking my practice afterwards. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep the paid repair role and use completed teaching only within the tasks and checks the supervisor authorised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but patient enough to learn. Five years gives me more time to repeat a practical task until I understand it. I don't want a screen telling me I've passed while the person checking the wiring still has to undo it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you pay the fee yourself if the employer refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could probably afford a modest fee. I wouldn't buy an electrical course with no clear place to practise the work. I'd ask the union to keep pressing for paid teaching and keep supervised work meanwhile. My preference for a shared agreement isn't a claim that my account is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expect the class to protect you after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the robots in your picture can do hands-on work too. The class could help me earn and contribute before then, and perhaps judge a new role more honestly. It can't turn an uncertain future into a written guarantee.

say: I'd use **five years** for employer-supported practical learning available beyond workers with private savings.
I'd explain **robots around 2034** still follow thinking AI rather than promise a permanently safe skill.
think: My **near-term income** looks secure while I have time to improve under supervision.
At **48** in 2031, I'll still need wages for a growing family beyond the first AI date.
do: Request the next **installation class** now as part of my paid week.
Enrol only with agreed **fees and paid time**, followed by a named senior checking practice.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031, using completed teaching only within authorised tasks and required checks.
feel: **Uneasy** about later competition, with patience and financial space for repeated practical learning.
S3.quote: I wouldn't buy an electrical course with no clear place to practise the work.
fieldNote: His **funding preference** is an equitable and practical choice despite affordability, not a false claim that the strong cushion prevents any self-funding.
He retains **supervision after class** and explicitly rejects permanent protection from the later robots, preserving the common scenario endpoint.

steps.text: Enrol in installation class only with agreed fees and paid time plus supervised practice
Keep authorised supervised repair work after 2031
Press for shared paid teaching through the union if employer funding is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough warning to build proper arrangements for people, not just budgets for equipment. I'd keep learning the physical trade in the way I know. I'd also ask who is making sure the worker without savings gets teaching before a change in hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own next few years feel secure because we can cover the mortgage and have a year's reserve. I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so I still wouldn't assume retirement had solved things. The wider change stays on my mind even when I don't fear this month's bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep requesting the paid installation class now, enrolling only with the agreed fees, paid hours and supervised practice. I'd attend the union meeting each quarter to follow the actual training agreement rather than buy software I'd avoid using. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid electrical work where offered and compare real hours and pay with the household budget before making any decision to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the bigger change, but comfortable about our current household position. Having more time doesn't make me keen to hand my learning over to AI. It gives me room to ask for a fair arrangement without pretending my own family has nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the quarterly meeting need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many workers actually received paid teaching, the hours covered and what paid work followed. A poster with a smiling apprentice doesn't show who received paid teaching. I'd read the figures on paper and ask about anyone left waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about your own longer future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I expect to keep working, but I won't promise the same job at the same wage forever. We'd check what we actually had saved and what the mortgage still cost. I wouldn't tell the children a pension payment was guaranteed when I hadn't checked the terms.

say: I'd use **ten years** to build fair training arrangements as well as equipment budgets.
I'd keep asking whether **workers without savings** receive teaching before hours change.
think: Our **mortgage and reserve** make my own next few years feel secure.
I still need **earnings after 2036**, and broader worker changes remain on my mind without assumed retirement.
do: Request the **installation class** now and enrol only with agreed fees, paid hours and supervised practice.
Attend **quarterly union meetings** to check who actually receives paid teaching and what work follows.
Keep **paid work** after 2036 and compare actual hours and pay with the budget before leaving.
feel: **Uneasy** about wider change, with his own present work and household finances feeling secure.
S4.quote: A poster with a smiling apprentice doesn't show who received paid teaching.
fieldNote: He separates **own security** from continuing concern about access to paid teaching, without borrowing a panic level from less secure households.
The **longer timeline** preserves resistance to AI, practical supervision and unchecked pension terms rather than assuming guaranteed retirement income.

steps.text: Take installation class only with agreed fees, paid hours and supervised practice
Attend quarterly union meetings to check actual paid teaching and subsequent work
Keep paid electrical work after 2036 while comparing actual hours with household costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robots follow around 2031 while I'm still building practical skill. A written paid-training and redeployment agreement with actual roles, hours and pay would help. I'd want the worker with no reserve to be able to use it as well as me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is checking whether promised teaching really happens. A training budget on paper isn't the same as a worker getting paid to learn. I can wait longer than some people, but that shouldn't be the test of who gets a future.

headlineQuote: A training budget on paper isn't the same as a worker getting paid to learn.
portrait: Omar is **43**, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and higher starter pay despite needing supervision.
He has a **partner and two children**, a mortgage, a year's expenses saved from two wages, and plentiful local firms.
He has **never used AI**, preferring paper drawings and patient instruction while pursuing paid teaching through union meetings and written requests.
Short timelines raise **own-hours risk**; longer ones preserve concern for shared access to training without pretending his strong reserve is absent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little practical-learning time before capable robots follow around 2031 and could reduce his paid hours.
whatWouldHelp: A written **paid-training agreement** with actual roles, hours and pay would support a usable route through change.
Equal **access to teaching** would let workers without private reserves use that route too.
